content: 1. Only 31% of clients who underwent circumcision through conventional surgical methods exhibited a regular and aesthetically pleasing appearance after four weeks. This was primarily attributed to the use of circumferential sutures. Long-term outcomes were not reported. 2. Pain was systematically assessed using a visual analogue scale during the procedure, immediately postoperatively, and within the first 24 and 48 hours after the procedure. Pain scores were comparable to those reported in the surgical arms of randomized controlled trials. 3. The circumcision procedure using a surgical assist device can be completed in a single visit. In contrast, other device-based methods require the device to remain on the penis for up to one week to achieve hemostasis, after which it must be removed. 4. Wound healing following the use of the surgical assist device is rapid and comparable to healing after conventional surgical circumcision. The cosmetic outcome is a neat, uniform wound without visible signs of recent suturing. 5. To date, the surgical assist device has been used by a limited number of experienced physicians. Further data is needed to evaluate the safety of this device when used by mid-level clinicians. Additionally, programmatic considerations such as training and other requirements need to be explored. 6. In a study involving local anesthesia, two out of 118 clients experienced transient pain during the application of maximum crushing force to the foreskin. However, the intensity of the pain was not reported. Adequate pain control was achieved with topical anesthesia applied for at least 25 minutes before the procedure. 7. Across studies, 93% of clients circumcised with the device were fully healed by four weeks. In comparative studies, nearly 90% of clients circumcised with the device and 89% of those circumcised with conventional surgery were healed by four weeks. Observational cohorts reported a 95% healing rate. 8. National programs must lead and coordinate with key stakeholders to adopt and scale up device-based circumcision methods. Clear communication of evidence, advantages, and disadvantages is essential. 9. A phased approach should be used to implement prequalified devices, starting with pilot or demonstration sites. These projects assess feasibility and refine usage through ongoing learning processes. 10. Health systems must be prepared to ensure the safe provision of the new method and maintain sufficient supply. Governments may rely on WHO prequalification to guide decisions on premarket approval, licensing, and importation. 11. Policies and regulations affecting the adoption of prequalified devices should be reviewed to expedite progress while ensuring safety. This includes premarket approval, licensing of manufacturers, post-market surveillance, and authorization of healthcare providers to use specific device methods. 12. Prequalified devices have been shown to achieve safe circumcision when used by appropriately trained and competent staff in well-equipped settings. However, manufacturer instructions alone are insufficient for competent performance. Device-specific clinical guidelines and standardized competency-based training are essential. 13. Facilities, equipment, and commodities required for device placement and removal will depend on the type of device used. The use of device-based methods does not eliminate the need for surgical services for ineligible clients, rare complications, or those preferring conventional methods. 14. Clients must receive the minimum service package, proper education, and counseling to provide informed consent. For in situ devices, a second visit may be required for device removal, necessitating service organization to accommodate two visits one week apart. 15. Men and their partners should be informed about the risks and benefits of the specific method. For in situ devices, clients must commit to wearing the device for one week, abstaining from sexual activity during the healing period (6–7 weeks), not removing the device themselves, and attending follow-up visits as required. 16. A reliable procurement and supply management system is needed to ensure consistent supply. Costs, logistics, commodities, and waste management requirements must be estimated. Device procurement challenges include stocking multiple sizes and ensuring availability of unique accessories and supplies. 17. Monitoring and evaluation are critical as large-scale rollout of devices has not yet occurred. Early monitoring in routine service settings will provide more information on safety and usage before wider implementation. 18. National programs bear the primary responsibility for recording and reporting adverse events. Mechanisms must be in place to monitor safety and share information about adverse events or device-related incidents with manufacturers and the WHO prequalification team. 19. Active surveillance should be conducted as devices are introduced in non-research settings, with proactive follow-up of clients. Once adverse event rates are deemed low by an independent group, active surveillance may transition to passive monitoring. 20. Research is needed to assess the effectiveness and efficiency of device-based methods, including reduced procedure time, costs, and acceptability to providers and clients. Further studies should explore the use of surgical assist devices by non-physician providers and evaluate training and implementation requirements. 21. Pain management, particularly with new or revised methods, requires further research. A consistent method for pain control using topical anesthesia needs to be clarified, especially for topical lidocaine, as only EMLA has been studied with the no-flip technique. 22. The safety of alternative ring sizes with the collar clamp should be documented in program monitoring. Service delivery models for specific circumcision methods and a mix of methods should also be explored. 23. To achieve 2030 HIV prevention targets, programs must focus on populations at higher risk of infection, such as partners of sex workers, men in serodiscordant relationships, and men attending STI clinics. Early efforts focused on generating demand for VMMC through communication strategies and raising awareness. 24. A more strategic and holistic approach is now needed, addressing both demand and supply factors. This includes tailoring interventions to the realities of adolescent boys and men, addressing barriers, and leveraging facilitators to increase service uptake. 25. Effective service coverage requires ensuring that all people have access to needed health services of sufficient quality without financial hardship. VMMC services must be reoriented and expanded to offer sexual and reproductive health and other life-course-relevant services to men. 26. Barriers to VMMC uptake include limited service availability and accessibility, as well as client knowledge, risk perception, and self-efficacy. Evidence-based interventions must address these barriers and facilitators to increase uptake among adolescent boys and men. 27. Common factors facilitating VMMC uptake include support from family and peers, knowledge of HIV and STI prevention, and understanding of improved penile hygiene and reduced health risks.
